Man, 70 years old, left colon tumor, three liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 200 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. MRI: invasion of the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular involvement, significant technical risk, volume to be assessed.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The hepatic lesions involve the hepatic vein confluence, creating a high‑risk vascular scenario that may be surgically addressed only after confirming that an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved and that liver function is sufficient. The missing quantitative FLR assessment (and functional reserve) is a decisive factor; without it the safety of an extended hepatectomy with venous reconstruction cannot be guaranteed. Therefore resection is possible but contingent on obtaining this information (or on performing a preparatory maneuver such as portal vein embolization if the FLR is insufficient).

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic therapy immediately: 6‑8 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given the left‑sided, RAS‑wild‑type primary.  
- Re‑stage with contrast‑enhanced MRI and volumetric CT after chemotherapy to evaluate tumor response and to calculate FLR volume.  
- If FLR is <30 % of total liver volume (or <40 % in a steatotic liver), proceed with portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments to be resected, aiming to hypertrophy the future remnant to a safe threshold.  
- Re‑image 4‑6 weeks after PVE to confirm adequate hypertrophy.  
- If disease remains limited to the liver and FLR is now adequate, plan a two‑stage surgical approach:  
   • Stage 1: Right/extended right hepatectomy (or appropriate anatomical resection) with en‑bloc resection of the involved hepatic vein confluence and reconstruction using a prosthetic or autologous graft, performed by an experienced hepatobiliary team.  
   • Stage 2 (within 2‑4 weeks): Left‑sided colectomy with primary anastomosis, unless the primary tumor has already been resected or is amenable to a simultaneous approach.  
- If intra‑operative assessment reveals unresectable vascular involvement or insufficient margins, abort hepatic resection and continue systemic therapy.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (additional 3‑6 months) to eradicate microscopic disease, with surveillance CEA and imaging every 3‑6 months.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and functional reserve (ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh, bilirubin).  
- Detailed anatomical relationship of each metastasis to the hepatic veins, portal branches, and biliary ducts.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., peritoneal, pulmonary).  
- Performance status and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Exact T‑stage and nodal status of the left‑colon primary.  
- Baseline liver parenchyma quality (steatosis, fibrosis).  
- Patient’s preferences regarding staged versus simultaneous resections.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases and MRI evidence of invasion of the hepatic vein confluence, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is limited, involvement of the venous outflow confluence makes a safe R0 resection with preservation of adequate hepatic venous drainage technically uncertain at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing and expert vascular reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and potential reduction of venous involvement.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Expert HPB/vascular and volumetric restaging
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the hepatic vein confluence.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) and evaluate feasibility of venous preservation or need for reconstruction.

E. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• If significant regression occurs, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection with the aim of R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible venous reconstruction or complex vascular control.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

F. Management of primary tumor
• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Precise relationship of each lesion to the hepatic vein confluence on MRI.
B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the three lesions.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, right T3N1M1 colon cancer, four liver metastases (3-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 780 ng/mL, non-V600E BRAF mutation (D594G).
MDT Discussion: Atypical BRAF mutation, intermediate prognosis, bilobar liver involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The case lacks critical information on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, hepatic functional reserve (Child‑Pugh, ICG clearance), and precise anatomical relationship of the four 3‑5 cm lesions to major vessels and biliary structures.  
- Bilobar disease with lesions of this size often requires volumetric assessment, possible portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage/ALPPS approach to achieve an adequate FLR.  
- Until these data are obtained, definitive upfront resection cannot be confirmed; however, the disease is not clearly unresectable, so it is classified as potentially resectable pending the prerequisite assessments.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy with an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) tailored to BRAF‑mutated colorectal cancer; consider adding a BRAF‑targeted agent if molecular board deems appropriate for non‑V600E mutation.  
- Re‑stage with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI after 2–3 cycles to evaluate tumor response and to perform volumetric analysis of the liver.  
- If FLR ≥30 % (in a normal liver) or ≥40 % (in a steatotic/chemotherapy‑injured liver) and margins appear achievable, proceed to a liver‑first approach:  
   • If FLR is insufficient, perform portal vein embolization (or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS) to hypertrophy the future remnant.  
   • Once adequate FLR is confirmed, undertake curative‑intent liver resection—either a single extended hepatectomy if feasible, or a staged/combined right and left hepatectomy to clear all four lesions with negative margins.  
- After successful hepatic clearance, address the primary right colon tumor with a standard right hemicolectomy (simultaneous with liver surgery only if operative risk is acceptable and margins are clear).  
- Complete the treatment with postoperative (adjuvant) systemic therapy, adapting the regimen based on pathological response and molecular profile.  
- Throughout, monitor CEA trends and perform surveillance imaging at regular intervals.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative liver volumetry (FLR percentage) and functional reserve (Child‑Pugh, ICG clearance, MELD).  
- Exact segmental location of each hepatic metastasis and proximity to major vessels/bile ducts.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung, peritoneum) on full staging.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities affecting surgical risk.  
- KRAS/NRAS mutation status (relevant for targeted therapy decisions).  
- Prior treatments received (if any) and response to initial systemic therapy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases (3–5 cm) in the setting of a right T3N1 colon cancer and elevated CEA (780 ng/mL). Despite bilobar distribution, the limited number of lesions suggests that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. The presence of a non-V600E BRAF D594G mutation is associated with a more indolent biology compared with V600E and does not contraindicate surgical intent. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Short peri-operative systemic therapy (recommended)
• Given the high CEA and bilobar disease, administer 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections of all four lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to optimize margins and preserve parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

E. Management of primary tumor
• Perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (2-4 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 320 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. Positive circulating tumor cells detected.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: Six liver metastases 2‑4 cm each are present, but the CT report does not specify their segmental distribution, relationship to major hepatic veins/portal structures, or the calculated future liver remnant (FLR). Without volumetric analysis and functional liver reserve assessment, it is impossible to confirm that an oncologically adequate and technically safe resection can be performed. Therefore a prerequisite step—detailed hepatic volumetry and functional testing (e.g., ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh, liver stiffness) or neoadjuvant systemic therapy to downsize lesions—must be completed before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy: FOLFOXIRI (5‑FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type left‑sided disease.  
- Re‑image the liver after 8–12 weeks (triphasic CT or MRI) to assess radiologic response, lesion shrinkage, and to obtain precise volumetric data.  
- Perform liver function assessment (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, platelet count) and calculate FLR. If FLR is <30 % in a normal liver (or <40 % in a steatotic/chemotherapy‑injured liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the lobe to be resected to induce hypertrophy.  
- Re‑evaluate resectability after chemotherapy ± PVE:  
   • If all lesions become resectable with an adequate FLR, schedule a staged approach—first colorectal primary resection (laparoscopic left hemicolectomy) followed by liver resection within 4–6 weeks, or a simultaneous resection if the hepatic procedure is limited to ≤3 segments and operative risk is acceptable.  
   • If only a subset of lesions can be cleared, consider a two‑step liver surgery (e.g., right hepatectomy followed by left lateral segmentectomy) after confirming sufficient FLR.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or continuation of oxaliplatin‑based therapy) for at least 3 months, given the high CEA, T4 primary, N2 nodes, and positive circulating tumor cells, to address micrometastatic disease.  
- Enroll in surveillance program: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced liver imaging every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Precise hepatic lesion mapping (segmental location, unilobar vs bilobar, proximity to major vessels/ducts).  
- Quantitative liver volumetry and calculation of future liver remnant.  
- Baseline liver function metrics (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, platelet count, Child‑Pugh score).  
- Performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum) not mentioned on current CT.  
- BRAF mutation status (important for prognosis and potential targeted therapy).  
- Details of prior or planned neoadjuvant therapy tolerance.
